messages.content: Make this more polite, please: Give me the salt. And close that window, it's cold.
Could you please pass me the salt? And would you mind closing the window? It's a bit cold in here.
Rewrite in the active voice: The window was broken by Arjun's cricket ball, and the glass was swept up by his grandmother.
Arjun's cricket ball broke the window, and his grandmother swept up the glass.
Put this into the past tense: Meera wakes up at six, drinks her chai and catches the 7:15 bus to college. She reads her notes on the way.
Meera woke up at six, drank her chai and caught the 7:15 bus to college. She read her notes on the way.
Can you make my message to my teacher more formal? "Hey sir, can't come tomorrow, got fever. Will send the work later. - Kabir"

Dear Sir,
I am unwell with a fever and will not be able to attend class tomorrow. I will send you the work as soon as I can. Thank you for understanding.
Yours sincerely,
Kabir
I'd like this to sound casual, like a text to a friend: I would like to inform you that I shall be arriving at the station at approximately half past four.
I'll get to the station at about half past four.
Shorten this sentence: Due to the fact that it was raining very heavily, we made the decision to postpone the picnic until a later date.
Because of the heavy rain, we put off the picnic.
Say it in simpler words: The municipal corporation has announced that water supply will be suspended on Thursday owing to maintenance work.
The city says there will be no water on Thursday because of repair work.
Please help me say this more kindly to my neighbour: Your dog barks all night. Stop it. I can't sleep.
I'm sorry to bother you, but your dog has been barking a lot at night, and I'm finding it hard to sleep. Could we talk about what might help?

Rewrite this diary entry in the third person and the past tense, about Swati:

Argued with Yogesh in the canteen about whether the state should fund private schools. He says yes; I say no. Instead of getting louder I asked, "How did you come to that view?"
Swati argued with Yogesh in the canteen about whether the state should fund private schools. He said yes, and she said no. Instead of getting louder, she asked him, "How did you come to that view?"

Make this shorter, in one sentence. The "she" is Xin.

At home she wrote a different message: "Honestly, when I don't hear back, I get scared you're losing interest. Could you just send a quick 'busy' when you are?" Then she went to choir practice, where she had a solo to learn, and forgot to check her phone for an hour.
At home, Xin sent a calm, honest message asking for a quick 'busy' text, then went to choir practice and forgot her phone for an hour.

Could you rewrite this in short, simple sentences for a young child? Pankaj is Hrithik's cousin.

Later, on the terrace where it was quieter, Hrithik told his mother he felt small, and she squeezed his shoulder and said marks were not all of him. He thought, I am more than a number, and went to find Pankaj.

Later, Hrithik went up to the quiet terrace. He told his mother he felt small. She squeezed his shoulder. She said marks are not everything about him. Hrithik thought, "I am more than a number." Then he went to find his cousin Pankaj.

Change this to the present tense and fix anything that sounds odd:

Shreya did not say "Let me play." Shreya held out a little plastic truck from the pocket and said, "I have a truck. It can go on your road." Santosh looked at it.
Shreya does not say, "Let me play." She holds out a little plastic truck from her pocket and says, "I have a truck. It can go on your road." Santosh looks at it.

Turn this dialogue into reported speech. "She" is Aditi.

"I do not know," Kishore admitted.
"Neither do I, it seems." She flipped her notes back. "I skipped collisions. Give me twenty minutes, and then let's try again."

Kishore admitted that he did not know. Aditi said that it seemed she did not know either. She flipped back through her notes and said that she had skipped collisions. She asked for twenty minutes, and then they would try again.

Say this in modern English:

It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.

However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.

Everyone seems to agree that a rich single man must be looking for a wife. When such a man moves to a new area, nobody knows much about his feelings or plans. Even so, the local families are so sure of this idea that each one sees him as a future husband for one of their daughters.

How would you write this in plain modern English for a young reader?

Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do: once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it, "and what is the use of a book," thought Alice "without pictures or conversations?"

Alice was getting very bored. She was sitting next to her sister on the bank with nothing to do. Once or twice she looked at her sister's book, but it had no pictures or conversations in it. "What is the use of a book without pictures or conversations?" Alice thought.

Please make this paragraph shorter and easier to read:

There was a table set out under a tree in front of the house, and the March Hare and the Hatter were having tea at it: a Dormouse was sitting between them, fast asleep, and the other two were using it as a cushion, resting their elbows on it, and talking over its head. "Very uncomfortable for the Dormouse," thought Alice; "only, as it's asleep, I suppose it doesn't mind."

The March Hare and the Hatter were having tea at a table under a tree. A Dormouse sat fast asleep between them, and they rested their elbows on it like a cushion. Alice thought this was uncomfortable for the Dormouse, but since it was asleep, it probably did not mind.

Put this passage into the present tense and plain, modern English:

It was another half-hour before I drew near to the kiln. The lime was burning with a sluggish stifling smell, but the fires were made up and left, and no workmen were visible. Hard by was a small stone-quarry. It lay directly in my way, and had been worked that day, as I saw by the tools and barrows that were lying about.

It is another half-hour before I get near the kiln. The lime is burning with a slow, choking smell. The fires have been built up and left, and I can see no workers. Close by is a small stone quarry. It lies right in my path, and people have worked in it today, because tools and wheelbarrows are lying around.

This is from an old detective story. Rewrite it in everyday English.

One morning, at a little before seven o'clock, I was awakened by the maid tapping at the door to announce that two men had come from Paddington and were waiting in the consulting-room. I dressed hurriedly, for I knew by experience that railway cases were seldom trivial, and hastened downstairs. As I descended, my old ally, the guard, came out of the room and closed the door tightly behind him.

One morning, just before seven, the maid knocked on my door to wake me. She said two men had come from Paddington and were waiting in the consulting room. I dressed quickly, because I knew from experience that railway cases were rarely small matters, and hurried downstairs. As I went down, my old friend the guard came out of the room and shut the door firmly behind him.

Modernise the language here, keeping the meaning:

Spring advanced rapidly; the weather became fine and the skies cloudless. It surprised me that what before was desert and gloomy should now bloom with the most beautiful flowers and verdure. My senses were gratified and refreshed by a thousand scents of delight and a thousand sights of beauty.

Spring came quickly. The weather turned fine and the sky was clear. I was surprised that land which had been bare and gloomy was now full of beautiful flowers and green plants. A thousand lovely smells and sights refreshed me and lifted my spirits.

What's a simpler way to say this?

My father yielded at length to my desire to avoid society and strove by various arguments to banish my despair. Sometimes he thought that I felt deeply the degradation of being obliged to answer a charge of murder, and he endeavoured to prove to me the futility of pride.

In the end, my father agreed to let me stay away from other people, and he tried in many ways to pull me out of my deep sadness. Sometimes he thought I felt ashamed because I had been put on trial for murder, and he tried to show me that this kind of pride was pointless.
